::: {.tutorial-meta}
**Level:** Beginner / Intermediate · **Working time:** 20 minutes
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Overview"}
* **Goal:** Keep configuration files synchronized across macOS and Linux computers without fragile symlinks.
* **Audience:** People who are new to dotfile managers or ChezMoi.
* **Outcome:** Understand why ChezMoi exists, how configuration moves between its three layers, and how to use it safely day to day.
* **Time required:** About 20 minutes for the first setup; a few minutes for normal updates.
* **Skill level:** Beginner / Intermediate.
* **Prerequisites:** A terminal, Git, a private Git repository, and ChezMoi.
* **Example:** Correct a typo in `~/.tmux.conf`, publish it, and safely apply it on a second Mac.
:::
Configuration files such as `.bashrc`, `.tmux.conf`, and application settings
are often called **dotfiles**. Copying them manually between computers works
for a while, but the copies eventually drift apart. Symlinking every live file
directly into a Git repository is better, but can become awkward when two
machines need slightly different settings.

[ChezMoi](https://www.chezmoi.io/) keeps a desired version of each managed
file in a source directory. It then previews and applies that desired state to
the normal file locations in your home directory.

---

## 1. The Problem: “Where Did I Put My Configuration?”

Imagine that you buy a new MacBook.

You install Ghostty. You install tmux, Emacs, and Git. Then you remember:

- Where is my `.tmux.conf`?
- What were my Git aliases?
- Which SSH hosts did I configure?
- Which font and colors did I use in Ghostty?
- Which parts should be the same as my Mac Mini?

You copy one file from Dropbox, another from GitHub, and a third from an old
laptop. Everything works—but each computer is now slightly different. Six
months later, you no longer know which copy is correct.

This is the problem ChezMoi solves:

> Keep one reviewed description of your configuration, then safely reproduce
> it on each computer.

ChezMoi is not primarily a backup program or a Git replacement. It is the
layer that understands how a stored configuration becomes a real file in your
home directory.

---

## 2. The Three Worlds

The easiest way to understand ChezMoi is to separate your configuration into
three layers:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    R["Remote Git repository<br>GitHub"]
    S["Source state<br>ChezMoi's desired configuration"]
    T["Target state<br>Live files in your home directory"]

    R -- "git pull" --> S
    S -- "git commit + push" --> R
    S -- "chezmoi apply" --> T
    T -- "chezmoi add / re-add" --> S
```

The arrows are intentional:

- `chezmoi apply` moves the desired configuration from the source state to
  the live target.
- `chezmoi add` begins managing a new live file by copying it into the source
  state.
- `chezmoi re-add` imports later edits from an already managed live file.
- Git synchronizes the source state between computers.

::: {.callout-tip title="Golden Rules"}
- Applications read configuration from your **home directory**, not from
  the ChezMoi source.
- Git synchronizes the **ChezMoi source**, not the live files.
- `chezmoi apply` updates live files from the source.
- `chezmoi re-add` imports edits from an already managed live file.
- Preview with `chezmoi diff` before moving changes in either direction.
:::
Four commands explain most daily state changes:

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `chezmoi status` | Summarize which live targets differ from the source |
| `chezmoi diff` | Preview what applying the source would change |
| `chezmoi apply` | Update live files from the source |
| `chezmoi re-add` | Import edits from an already managed live file |

You will also use `chezmoi add` once when introducing a new file and
`chezmoi edit` when editing the source directly.

### Target state: the files your programs use

The **target state** consists of the normal files in your home directory:

```text
~/.tmux.conf
~/.bashrc
~/.config/ghostty/config
~/.emacs.d/init.el
```

tmux reads `~/.tmux.conf`; Emacs reads files under `~/.emacs.d`; neither
program needs to know that ChezMoi exists.

### Source state: your tested save state

The **source state** is the desired version managed by ChezMoi. Think of it as
a tested save state or blueprint:

1. Experiment in the live environment.
2. Confirm that the configuration works.
3. Import the stable result with `chezmoi add` or `chezmoi re-add`.
4. Review it and commit it to Git.

Alternatively, edit the source first and apply it to the live environment for
testing. Both directions are explained later in this tutorial.

By default, ChezMoi stores its source under:

```text
~/.local/share/chezmoi/
```

This tutorial uses a custom source directory:

```text
~/developer/projects/my_config/home/
```

For the tmux example, the three layers are:

| Layer | Example path |
| --- | --- |
| Target/live file | `~/.tmux.conf` |
| ChezMoi source | `~/developer/projects/my_config/home/dot_tmux.conf` |
| Remote Git repository | A private repository on GitHub |

### Why these are copies rather than symlinks

Tools such as GNU Stow commonly make the live file a symlink pointing into a
Git repository. ChezMoi normally computes the desired contents and writes a
regular file at the target location instead.

This separation provides a useful safety boundary:

- breaking the live file does not immediately change the tracked source;
- a source edit does not affect the live program until you apply it;
- `chezmoi diff` lets you review the difference in either case; and
- backups and Git history provide additional recovery points.

The separation is not magic protection. `chezmoi apply` deliberately updates
the live file, and `chezmoi re-add` deliberately imports the live file into
the source. Preview the difference before running either command.

::: {.callout-note title="The repository is still necessary"}
Your live configuration continues to work temporarily without the
repository, but the repository is the source of truth used to synchronize,
review, reinstall, and recover the configuration.
:::
### Source files can contain machine-specific logic

The source state does not have to be an identical static copy for every
computer. ChezMoi templates can select values using properties such as the
operating system, hostname, or architecture.

For example, the same Emacs configuration can share its main initialization
while selecting a different local path on macOS and Ubuntu. Small local-only
files—such as `~/.emacs.d/local.el` or `~/.ssh/config.local`—can also remain
outside Git.

Templates are an advanced feature; the important idea for now is that one
source repository can safely produce slightly different target files on
different machines.

ChezMoi uses special source names. A few examples are:

| Source name | Target |
| --- | --- |
| `dot_tmux.conf` | `~/.tmux.conf` |
| `dot_bashrc` | `~/.bashrc` |
| `private_dot_ssh/private_config` | `~/.ssh/config` with private permissions |
| `private_dot_config/ghostty/config` | `~/.config/ghostty/config` |

---

## 3. Learn One Direction at a Time

Instead of memorizing every command, follow one configuration through three
days.

### Day 1: Start managing a file

Assume `~/.gitconfig` already exists and you have checked that it contains no
password or token:

```bash
chezmoi add ~/.gitconfig
```

Direction:

```text
HOME                              CHEZMOI SOURCE
~/.gitconfig  ───── add ─────▶    dot_gitconfig
```

What actually changed?

```text
Before:
  HOME:    ~/.gitconfig
  SOURCE:  no managed Git configuration

After:
  HOME:    ~/.gitconfig            (unchanged)
  SOURCE:  dot_gitconfig           (new desired copy)
```

`add` does not move or delete the live file. It begins managing it by creating
the source representation.

### Day 2: Change the desired configuration

Edit the source:

```bash
chezmoi edit ~/.gitconfig
```

The live file has not changed yet. Preview and apply:

```bash
chezmoi diff ~/.gitconfig
chezmoi apply ~/.gitconfig
```

Direction:

```text
CHEZMOI SOURCE                    HOME
dot_gitconfig  ──── apply ────▶   ~/.gitconfig
```

What actually changed?

```text
Before apply:
  SOURCE:  contains your new setting
  HOME:    still contains the old setting

After apply:
  SOURCE:  contains your new setting
  HOME:    now contains the new setting
```

### Day 3: Synchronize another computer

Commit and push the source repository:

```text
CHEZMOI SOURCE  ─── git push ───▶  GITHUB
```

On the other computer, pull and preview:

```text
GITHUB  ─── git pull ───▶  CHEZMOI SOURCE
```

Then apply:

```text
CHEZMOI SOURCE  ─── chezmoi apply ───▶  HOME
```

The key idea is repeated because it matters:

> Git synchronizes the ChezMoi source. ChezMoi installs that source into your
> home directory.

---

## 4. Why Not Use Git Alone?

A plain Git repository is excellent at storing history and moving files
between computers. It does not know where each file belongs in your home
directory or how that file should differ by machine.

| Git | ChezMoi |
| --- | --- |
| Versions and transfers files | Manages how source becomes live configuration |
| Sees repository paths | Maps source names to paths under `$HOME` |
| Preserves ordinary Git metadata | Can manage target permissions and file types |
| Stores the same committed text | Can render templates using OS, hostname, or architecture |
| Plain secrets are unsafe | Can integrate encryption or password managers |
| Does not install dotfiles | Previews and applies dotfiles |

::: {.callout-warning title="ChezMoi does not automatically make secrets safe"}
Encryption and password-manager integration must be configured
deliberately. A plain token added to the source is still a plain token in
Git.
:::
GitHub is the remote copy used for synchronization. The **local ChezMoi source
repository** is the working source of truth you review, edit, and commit.

---

## 5. What Should and Should Not Be Stored

| Usually manage | Manage selectively | Keep out of ChezMoi/Git |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.gitconfig` after review | Shared parts of SSH `config` | SSH private keys |
| `.tmux.conf` | Portable Karabiner rules | Tokens and passwords |
| Bash/Zsh configuration | VS Code settings without credentials | Histories and caches |
| Ghostty configuration | OS-specific application preferences | Browser/application databases |
| Authored Emacs configuration | Machine-local path fragments | Downloads and personal documents |
| Personal scripts without secrets | Public SSH keys if genuinely useful | Photos, movies, and backups |

ChezMoi is for authored configuration, not for backing up your entire home
directory.

Start with one or two files, verify the workflow, and expand gradually:

```bash
chezmoi add ~/.tmux.conf
chezmoi add ~/.config/ghostty/config
chezmoi add ~/.emacs.d/init.el
```

SSH configuration requires extra review:

```bash
chezmoi add ~/.ssh/config
```

Manage the configuration only—not private keys, `known_hosts`, agent sockets,
or control sockets.

::: {.callout-important title="Git history remembers secrets"}
Deleting a secret in a later commit does not remove it from earlier Git
history. If a credential is committed, rotate it immediately and clean the
repository history.
:::
For a small machine-specific difference, use a local file that is not managed
by ChezMoi. For example, a shared `~/.ssh/config` can contain:

```sshconfig
Include ~/.ssh/config.local
```

Each computer can then keep its private or machine-only host blocks in
`~/.ssh/config.local`.

---

## 6. A Small Command Map

```text
New unmanaged live file:
HOME  ─── chezmoi add ───▶  SOURCE

Edited managed live file:
HOME  ─── chezmoi re-add ───▶  SOURCE

Edited source file:
SOURCE  ─── chezmoi apply ───▶  HOME

Synchronize source:
SOURCE  ◀── git pull/push ──▶  GITHUB
```

You only need a few inspection commands:

```bash
chezmoi status
chezmoi diff
chezmoi verify
chezmoi source-path ~/.tmux.conf
```

`status` summarizes pending target changes. `diff` previews them. `verify`
checks that live files match the desired state. `source-path` answers “where
is the source for this live file?”

---

## 7. Two Valid Editing Workflows

The important question is: **did you edit the source file or the live file?**

### Workflow A: Edit the ChezMoi source

This is the recommended workflow:

```bash
chezmoi edit ~/.tmux.conf
```

Saving the editor changes the source, but not the live file. Applying can
happen immediately or later:

```bash
chezmoi diff ~/.tmux.conf
chezmoi apply ~/.tmux.conf
chezmoi verify ~/.tmux.conf
```

To edit and apply in one operation:

```bash
chezmoi edit --apply ~/.tmux.conf
```

`--apply` is only a convenience. Editing and applying do not have to happen at
the same time.

### Workflow B: Edit the live file

Sometimes you naturally open and save the normal file:

```bash
${EDITOR:-vi} ~/.tmux.conf
```

The live file has changed, but the ChezMoi source is still old. Import the live
version back into the source:

```bash
chezmoi diff ~/.tmux.conf
chezmoi re-add ~/.tmux.conf
chezmoi verify ~/.tmux.conf
```

You do not need `chezmoi apply` in this workflow because the live file already
contains the change.

::: {.callout-warning title="Templates are different"}
`chezmoi re-add` is not suitable for templated files. For templates, edit
the source template or use `chezmoi merge`.
:::
The two directions are:

```text
Edit source file → chezmoi apply
Edit live file   → chezmoi re-add
```

---

## 8. Real Example: Fix `~/.tmux.conf` and Synchronize It

Assume the first Mac uses this ChezMoi source repository:

```text
~/developer/projects/my_config
```

Suppose you directly edited `~/.tmux.conf`, corrected a typo, and saved it.

### Step 1: Preview the live/source difference

```bash
chezmoi diff ~/.tmux.conf
```

In the real example, the intended correction was:

```diff
-set -ag terminal-overrides ",xterm-256color:Cc=\E]12;%p1%s\7"
+set -ag terminal-overrides ",xterm-256color:Cc=\e]12;%p1%s\a"
```

Review the complete output. Stop if unrelated settings also changed.

### Step 2: Import the saved live file

```bash
chezmoi re-add ~/.tmux.conf
```

This copies the current live file into ChezMoi's source representation.

### Step 3: Verify and test

```bash
chezmoi verify ~/.tmux.conf

tmux -L chezmoi-check -f ~/.tmux.conf \
  start-server \; show -gv default-terminal \; kill-server
```

The test starts an isolated tmux server, reads the file, prints the configured
terminal type, and stops the test server.

### Step 4: Review the Git change

```bash
git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config diff -- \
  home/dot_tmux.conf
```

Confirm that the diff contains only the intended correction.

### Step 5: Commit and push

```bash
git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config add -- \
  home/dot_tmux.conf

git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config commit \
  -m "Fix typo in tmux config"

git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config push
```

The correction is now stored on GitHub. The second computer has not changed
yet.

---

## 9. Apply the Change on the Second Computer

### Step 1: Pull without creating a merge commit

```bash
git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config pull --ff-only
```

If this cannot fast-forward, stop and inspect the second computer's repository
instead of forcing the pull.

### Step 2: Preview before applying

```bash
chezmoi diff ~/.tmux.conf
```

This should show the same one-line correction. The live file is still
unchanged.

### Step 3: Make a timestamped backup

```bash
dotfiles_stamp="$(date '+%Y%m%dT%H%M%S%z')"
dotfiles_backup="$HOME/dotfiles-backups/${dotfiles_stamp}/tmux"

mkdir -p "$dotfiles_backup"
chmod 700 "$dotfiles_backup"
cp -Pp "$HOME/.tmux.conf" "$dotfiles_backup/.tmux.conf"
```

Keep this backup until the new configuration has been tested.

### Step 4: Apply only tmux

```bash
chezmoi apply ~/.tmux.conf
```

This does not apply Bash, SSH, Ghostty, or Emacs changes.

### Step 5: Verify

```bash
chezmoi verify ~/.tmux.conf
chezmoi status ~/.tmux.conf
```

No output means the source and live file match.

If tmux is installed, validate and reload it:

```bash
tmux -L chezmoi-check -f ~/.tmux.conf \
  start-server \; show -gv default-terminal \; kill-server

tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf
```

The first command validates in an isolated server. The second reloads the file
in an existing tmux server.

The completed path was:

```text
live file on Mac 1
  → chezmoi re-add
  → Git commit and push
  → Git pull on Mac 2
  → chezmoi diff
  → backup
  → chezmoi apply
  → verify
```

---

## 10. Setting Up a New Computer

For a conventional ChezMoi repository:

```bash
chezmoi init git@github.com:YOUR_USER/YOUR_DOTFILES_REPOSITORY.git
chezmoi diff
chezmoi apply
chezmoi verify
```

Do not use `init --apply` on a computer that already has valuable
configuration files. Inspect and back them up first.

If you deliberately keep the source in a custom directory such as
`~/developer/projects/my_config`, clone it there and configure ChezMoi's
`sourceDir`:

```bash
git clone git@github.com:YOUR_USER/YOUR_DOTFILES_REPOSITORY.git \
  "$HOME/developer/projects/my_config"

mkdir -p "$HOME/.config/chezmoi"
chmod 700 "$HOME/.config/chezmoi"
```

Create `~/.config/chezmoi/chezmoi.toml`:

```toml
sourceDir = "/Users/YOUR_USER/developer/projects/my_config"
```

On Linux the absolute path will normally be `/home/YOUR_USER/...`.

Then inspect and apply files individually:

```bash
chezmoi source-path
chezmoi status
chezmoi diff
chezmoi apply ~/.tmux.conf
chezmoi verify ~/.tmux.conf
```

Restore SSH keys, tokens, and machine-local files separately through a secure
channel. They should not come from the Git repository.

---

## 11. Common Beginner Mistakes

### “I edited a live file, but Git shows nothing”

If the file is already managed, ChezMoi's source still contains the old
version:

```bash
chezmoi diff ~/.bashrc
chezmoi re-add ~/.bashrc
git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config diff
```

Use `chezmoi add` instead when the live file has never been managed.

### “I edited the source, but the program still uses the old setting”

The source changed; the target did not:

```bash
chezmoi diff ~/.bashrc
chezmoi apply ~/.bashrc
```

### “My other laptop cannot see the change”

Check whether you committed and pushed:

```bash
git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config status
git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config log -1 --oneline
git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config push
```

Then pull on the receiving computer.

### “I pulled the commit, but the application did not change”

Git updated the source repository, not the live file:

```bash
chezmoi diff
chezmoi apply ~/.tmux.conf
```

Some applications must also reload their configuration. For example:

```bash
tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf
```

### “GitHub is my live configuration”

It is not. GitHub stores the remote Git copy. The local ChezMoi repository is
the source you edit and review; `chezmoi apply` produces the live
configuration.

### “I ran `chezmoi apply` without reviewing”

Preview first, especially on an existing computer:

```bash
chezmoi status
chezmoi diff
chezmoi apply --dry-run --verbose
```

Back up valuable existing files and apply one target at a time.

### “I committed a private key or token”

Removing it in the next commit is not enough. Stop publishing, rotate or
revoke the credential, and clean the Git history. ChezMoi does not turn a
plain secret into an encrypted secret automatically.

---

## 12. Emacs and “Waiting for Emacs…”

ChezMoi uses `$VISUAL` or `$EDITOR`. If it is configured as `emacsclient`, an
Emacs server must be running.

Inside Emacs:

```text
M-x server-start RET
```

From the terminal:

```bash
emacsclient --eval '(emacs-pid)'
EDITOR="emacsclient -c" chezmoi edit ~/.tmux.conf
```

After editing:

1. Save with `C-x C-s`.
2. Finish the client edit with `C-x #`.

`C-x #` is important: it tells the waiting `emacsclient` process that editing
is complete.

If editor integration is inconvenient, open the source file directly:

```bash
emacsclient -c \
  ~/developer/projects/my_config/home/dot_tmux.conf
```

After saving it, run:

```bash
chezmoi diff ~/.tmux.conf
chezmoi apply ~/.tmux.conf
```

---

## 13. The Typical Daily Workflow

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    E["Edit one configuration"]
    D["chezmoi diff"]
    A["chezmoi apply<br>or chezmoi re-add"]
    V["Test and verify"]
    C["git commit"]
    P["git push"]

    E --> D --> A --> V --> C --> P
```

Which ChezMoi command you use depends on where you edited:

```text
Edited SOURCE?  Preview → apply → test → commit → push
Edited HOME?    Preview → re-add → test → commit → push
```

On the computer where you make the change:

```bash
chezmoi status
chezmoi diff
chezmoi verify
git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config status
git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config diff
```

Commit and push only reviewed source files.

On the receiving computer:

```bash
git -C ~/developer/projects/my_config pull --ff-only
chezmoi status
chezmoi diff
chezmoi apply ~/.tmux.conf
chezmoi verify ~/.tmux.conf
```

For a faster trusted workflow, `chezmoi update` can pull and apply in one
command. On important machines, the explicit `pull → diff → backup → apply`
sequence is easier to audit and recover.

---

## 14. The 30-Second Mental Model

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    HA["Machine A<br>HOME"]
    SA["Machine A<br>ChezMoi source"]
    G["GitHub"]
    SB["Machine B<br>ChezMoi source"]
    HB["Machine B<br>HOME"]

    HA -- "add / re-add" --> SA
    SA -- "git push" --> G
    G -- "git pull" --> SB
    SB -- "apply" --> HB
```

Remember four directions:

```text
HOME     ── add/re-add ──▶  CHEZMOI
CHEZMOI  ───── apply ────▶  HOME
CHEZMOI  ─── git push ───▶  GITHUB
GITHUB   ─── git pull ───▶  CHEZMOI
```

Everything else in ChezMoi—templates, encryption, OS detection, external
password managers—is a variation built on this model.

> Git moves the source between machines. ChezMoi moves the source into HOME.
